term and the future are not only periods of time which stand
at our disposal for the realization of our plans, they are also
waves in the onward sweep of the time stream.
If we carefully consider this, we shall also begin to realize
that the chief point is not what we have accomplished by
our trouble in the past term and how we propose to build
further on this basis, but what, while doing our work, has
been happening to our selves and what is to emerge from
these hidden selves of ours, in the sense which the poet has
in mind when he speaks of our growing ripe for death. But
how could we become ripe for death and eternity if eternity
itself did not already determine our life in time, did not
limit and judge our work in time? If in the flux of time we
did not in some sense participate in eternity? Whence shall
we gain this assurance?
In this hour of evening worship we must allow a word of
the eternal God to strike home to us. Which word shall it be?
How are we to choose among the riches of the words of
Scripture, without running the risk of selecting a word
which is in harmony with our mood, and with those secret
wishes hidden in our mood? The New Testament contains
no word which has a direct bearing on a situation such as is
ours to-day; it contains no word which alludes to specific
turning points of time, whether those which nature has fixed
such as morning and evening, or the course of the year and
its seasons; or the beginning and end of those periods into
which time is divided for the organization of our human work.
The New Testament pays no attention to these time
periods which are so significant to us. It knows only one
critical turning point of time—when the "time was fulfilled";
it knows only one "now" which in human life is lifted above
the stream of time—the "now" when the word of God
strikes a man and which becomes for him the decisive
moment between time and eternity.
